name: Ben Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are lectures on animal biology and anatomy, afternoons are labs or the library, and twice a week I get up at six to help at the university farm, which is the best part. I'm doing veterinary science, so there are lots of terms to memorise: bones, muscles, hormones, you name it. I share a house with four other lads, two of them on my course, and we mostly live on pasta and tinned beans. My family runs a dairy farm about two hours away, and my dad rings me every Sunday to tell me what the herd's been up to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, there's always a new gadget and half of them don't last. I'd tell the lads on the course that animals still need people with strong hands and a good eye. I'd probably say it over a pint and not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be glad. A plateau means farming and vet work carry on as they are, and that's the future I signed up for. I'd keep my head down, pass my exams, and hope the milk price holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up lectures and farm mornings, go home most holidays to help with calving, and apply for a summer placement at a mixed practice. I'd keep saving a bit from the farm-hand pay my dad gives me. I wouldn't change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My parents are paying for the degree, I have good grades, and I know the work. I'm lucky in that, and my dad reminds me not to forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on. What would your dad say about a plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price, mostly. My dad checks the milk price like other people check football scores, and when it dips, the whole house goes quiet. A plateau doesn't fix that, and I worry about it more than about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything on the farm that's already worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, good, I told you so, and then he'd ask me to come home for a weekend to help with the hay. He's not a man for big ideas. He believes in work and weather.

say: I'd say there's **always a new gadget** and half don't last.
I'd say animals still need people with **a good eye**.
think: Privately I'm **glad**: farming and vet work carry on as they are.
I worry more about the **milk price** than about robots.
do: Keep up lectures and **farm mornings**, and go home to help with calving.
Apply for a summer placement at a **mixed practice** and keep saving.
feel: **Calm**, lucky to have my parents' backing.
S0.quote: My dad checks the milk price like other people check football scores, and when it dips, the whole house goes quiet.
fieldNote: His **milk price worry** exists whatever AI does.
He holds a **work-and-weather** view passed on by his father.
He keeps talk **to friends**, not online.

steps.text: Go home most holidays to help with calving and hay
Apply for a summer placement at a mixed veterinary practice
Save part of the farm-hand pay my dad gives me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing if it saves time and keeps costs down, but only if farmers aren't forced to buy expensive kit. I'd tell my mates that new tools are fine as long as they work. I'd say it plainly and then get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm pretty steady. A vet's job is mostly hands and eyes: examining animals, doing procedures, calming a farmer. The paperwork and the ordering and the records will be taken over first, and good riddance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI a bit more, for records and for summarising papers, but keep checking it. I'd ask the university farm manager what systems they use, and see which ones actually work. I'd talk to my dad about whether the farm should try a feed-planning app, since he'd never ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of caution. It sounds like useful change, not a crisis. I'd just hope the big firms don't take all the benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a vet's day do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Records, stock ordering, booking appointments, and reading test results. A vet in a mixed practice told me she spends the evenings on paperwork after a long day. If software could take that, she'd happily pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change on your dad's farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm already has a robotic milker. My dad grumbled about the robotic milker for two years and now wouldn't give it up, so he trusts what he sees. Software would handle more of the herd records and feed planning, and he'd be sceptical until it saved him an hour.

say: I'd say it's good if it saves time and **keeps costs down**.
I'd say new tools are fine, **as long** as they work.
think: Privately I'm **steady**: a vet's job is mostly hands and eyes.
Records and ordering go first, **good riddance**.
do: Use AI a bit more for **records** and papers, always checking it.
Ask my dad whether the farm should try a **feed-planning app**.
feel: **Calm** with some caution, because it sounds like useful change.
S1.quote: My dad grumbled about the robotic milker for two years and now wouldn't give it up, so he trusts what he sees.
fieldNote: He sees **paperwork** as the first thing to go and welcomes it.
The farm's **robotic milker** story shows how change really lands in his world.
He trusts **practical proof**, matching his steady adaptability.

steps.text: Use AI for records and summarising papers, always checking the results
Suggest a feed-planning app to my dad for the farm
Keep working weekends at the university farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need sensible planning and honest information, and that rules should help small farms and local vets, not just big firms. I'd say it to the vet association, as a student member. I'd not post anything, because I wouldn't know enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be rattled. If AI can do all the thinking work in two years, I'd be in my second year at a time when everything shifts, and I'd wonder if the money my parents are spending is a good bet. I'd also worry about my dad, because milk and feed prices depend on all sorts of systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my dad first and ask what he thinks, then talk to my tutor and the vet association. I'd stay in the degree, because animals still need hands, but I'd try to get more practical placements. I'd also look at whether the farm could cut costs, and I'd learn how to use the AI tools properly so I'm not behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. I'd keep myself busy and make jokes, but I'd be worried at night. I'd remind myself that animals still need a vet, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: what's the first call you make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably safer than most jobs, because robots need to be good enough to handle live animals, which is hard. But about 2031 it might be a different story, and I'd graduate around then. I'd want to make sure I'm good at the things a robot can't do easily, like calming a nervous cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does a vet's job look to you once robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on my practical skills: handling animals, doing real procedures, working in difficult conditions. A calf doesn't read the chatbot's advice, so the person standing in the cold shed at three in the morning is the one who counts. That's the person I'd aim to be.

say: I'd say we need **honest information**, and rules that help small farms.
I'd say it to the **vet association**, not online.
think: Privately I'd be **rattled**: I'd wonder if my parents' money is a good bet.
I'd also worry about my **dad**, since milk and feed prices depend on systems.
do: Ring my dad, then my tutor and the **vet association**.
Seek more **practical placements** and learn the AI tools properly.
feel: **Anxious**, joking by day and worrying at night.
S2.quote: A calf doesn't read the chatbot's advice, so the person standing in the cold shed at three in the morning is the one who counts.
fieldNote: He compares his **vet future** to the cold shed, a vivid image of hands-on worth.
His fear includes **his father's farm**, not just his own career.
He hedges by getting **more practical placements**.

steps.text: Ring my dad, then my tutor and the vet association for advice
Get more practical placements on farms and in mixed practices
Learn the AI tools properly so I'm not behind
Work out with my dad where the farm could cut costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get this right, but only if people stop talking and start doing. I'd say the farming unions should be at the table, and so should students. I'd turn up to a meeting if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy but hopeful. Five years takes me through most of my degree, and I'd start work around the time robots appear. That's a good bit of runway, and I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take as many placements as I can, and learn the AI tools to the point where I can use them confidently. I'd talk to my dad about investing a bit in the farm, maybe sensors or feed software, once we've seen what works. I'd save, too, in case the first few years of practice are tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd be getting on with things. I've always worked better when I have something to do with my hands, and this gives me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if it can be made to pay. Farms like ours depend on being efficient, and technology can help with that, so my brother and I might actually find it easier to run. But I'd want to see numbers before I'd bet the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the farm stay in the family in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep an eye on who's selling what. I'd rather be careful than first, because half of the farm technology out there is sold to farmers who don't need it.

say: I'd say there's time, but people must **start doing**, not talking.
I'd say **farming unions** should be at the table, and students.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy but hopeful**: five years is a good bit of runway.
I'd want **numbers** before betting the farm on technology.
do: Take **placements** and learn the AI tools to use them confidently.
Talk to my dad about a small **farm investment** such as sensors, once we've seen what works.
feel: **Uneasy**, but getting on with things, which suits me.
S3.quote: I'd rather be careful than first, because half of the farm technology out there is sold to farmers who don't need it.
fieldNote: He **mistrusts hype** but accepts proven tools, a steady stance.
He imagines a **farm future** with his brother, a family anchor.
He wants **numbers** before any big spending.

steps.text: Take as many placements as I can through the degree
Learn the AI tools until I can use them confidently
Suggest to my dad a small, proven investment in sensors or feed software
Save part of my pay for the first practice years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the best thing is to keep farming and vet work strong. I'd say we should look after our rural towns and keep young people in the countryside. I'd keep my head down and do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. By 2036 I'd be 29 and a few years into practice, maybe with a share in a small clinic. The robots come after that, and by then I'd have my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work in a mixed practice, and learn the tools as they mature. I'd put money into the farm only when it makes sense, and I'd save for a house near my family. I'd probably take a leadership role at a local farmers' club, because we need younger voices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade seems like a lot of time. I'd get on with life, and maybe even enjoy the changes, if they make the work easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: does that feel like a different world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Ten years is long enough for things to change in ways nobody guessed, and a farm is a slow thing to turn around. But I'd rather deal with it as it comes than lose sleep now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who or what do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly big firms that squeeze small farms and policymakers who move too slowly. Farmers should speak up earlier, instead of grumbling in the yard afterwards, and that's the thing we need to change.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so keep farming and vet work strong.
I'd say we should keep **young people** in the countryside.
think: Privately I'm **calm**: I'd be 29 and a few years into practice.
The robots come after that, and I'd have my **feet under me**.
do: Finish my degree, work in a **mixed practice**, and learn tools as they mature.
Save for a **house** near my family and join a local farmers' club.
feel: **Calm**, since a decade seems like a lot of time.
S4.quote: Farmers should speak up earlier, instead of grumbling in the yard afterwards, and that's the thing we need to change.
fieldNote: His blame is aimed at **big firms** and slow policy, with some self-criticism of farmers.
He plans a **local role**, a traditional civic habit.
He wants to deal with it **as it comes**, not worry now.

steps.text: Work in a mixed practice after qualifying and learn tools as they mature
Save for a house near my family
Join a local farmers' club and speak up early on policy
Invest in the farm only when a proven tool pays for itself

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the farm and the practice that I want to work in would both be changing before I've qualified, and my dad is counting on me to understand it. What would help is practical stuff: honest advice from the vet association, and fair rules for small farms. I don't want handouts, I want a level field, so small farms aren't squeezed out by big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I do use AI a bit, mainly for drafting emails and summarising dry papers, but I check everything. A calf doesn't care what a chatbot said about it, and my dad would laugh me off the farm if I quoted a screen to him. I'd say most farm kids are like that: practical first, curious second.

headlineQuote: I don't want handouts, I want a level field, so small farms aren't squeezed out by big ones.
portrait: Ben is 19, in first-year **veterinary science**, with top results and a family dairy farm behind him.
He is traditional and steady: he uses AI **now and then** for emails and papers.
He cares about the **family farm**, free markets and a level field.
His mood stays calm in mild cases and tightens to **anxious** when the date is two years away.
He blames **big firms** and slow policy, and relies on his father and housemates.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because the farm and his career would both change before he qualifies.
whatWouldHelp: Practical **honest advice** from the vet association, not slogans.
**Fair rules** so small farms aren't squeezed out by big ones.
